title: Norway’s EUSBSR accession opens new opportunities for cooperation in education and social inclusion
content:
Norway’s full participation in the EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region (EUSBSR) was officially celebrated in Oslo on 16 October 2026. For Policy Area Education, the occasion was also an opportunity to strengthen dialogue with Norwegian stakeholders and explore new possibilities for cooperation on shared societal challenges.

Norway became the ninth participating country in the EUSBSR on 18 May 2026, marking an important step in strengthening cooperation across the Baltic Sea Region.

The official launch event in Oslo on 16 October brought together Norwegian Minister of Foreign Affairs Espen Barth Eide, Minister of Local Government and Regional Development Bjørnar Skjæran, representatives of the European Commission, Policy Area Coordinators and stakeholders from across the region.

The programme focused on Norway’s role in the Strategy, its longstanding experience of Baltic Sea cooperation and the opportunities that full participation creates for contributing to shared priorities.

title: Cohesion builds the precondition for a competitive Europe and the Baltic Sea Region
content:
The Baltic Sea Region, like all macro-regions, faces challenges that no country, region or city can tackle alone. Resilience, competitiveness, climate work and connectivity all require territorial solutions. This was the starting point for the session “Fit for purpose – EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region builds a competitive, prosperous and carbon neutral region” at the EU Week of Regions and Cities 2026.

The EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region Action Plan (2026, pending Commission approval) gave the framework for the discussion. The recently updated Action Plan is the most geographically and thematically comprehensive framework for transnational work in the Baltic Sea Region. The Member States of the Strategy highlight the urgent need to respond to challenges such as a rapidly evolving security environment and increasingly complex multi-hazard risks: accelerating climate change and persistent environmental pressures, demographic change, and the demands of the green and digital transitions.

title: Nautical Mail – Policy Area Ship Newsletter
content:
O-HOY and Welcome Dear Reader,

Enjoy the pleasure of viewing the latest Newsletter by the EU Strategy of the Baltic Sea Region Policy Area for Sustainable Shipping (SHIP)!

PA Ship News

Coordination of the PA Ship is changing. Finnish Transport and Communications Agency will pass over the role of the Policy Area Coordination to Kotka Maritime Research Center Merikotka from 1st of January 2027 onwards. Coordinators from Traficom will pass over all material and knowledge forward to the coordinators at Merikotka. We wish all the best and smooth sails to the new coordinators!

SAVING THE SEA – News from our Projects

Circular Ports

Circular Ports has had an active start to autumn! The project has been represented at several events around the Baltic Sea Region, while work continues with all six pilots.

In August, Circular Ports took part in the Europe Forum in Turku with the Harbours of Change: Circular Economy in Baltic Sea Ports session, bringing together perspectives from EUSBSR PA Ship, Port of Turku and Circular Ports pilots on practical circular economy solutions in port environments. Read more about the session and its key takeaways here.

title: Denmark focuses on building favourable preconditions for Action Plan implementation
content:
On 28 September, Denmark hosted the first official meeting of the EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region National Coordinators Group. This meeting, followed by a full working day with a wider stakeholder group, marked the kick-off of the Danish Presidency 2026-2027.

Denmark’s Presidency of the EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region focuses on:

  • Ensuring an effective start to the implementation phase of the updated Action Plan (2026, pending European Commission approval). The Presidency encourages Policy Areas to use the first implementation phase to prepare the ground for their Actions to be taken forward across the Baltic Sea Region, including by identifying relevant partners, funding opportunities, and cooperation links with programmes, organisations, and actors in the region.
  • Increased Ukrainian involvement in the Strategy where relevant.
    The Presidency encourages Policy Areas and Steering Groups to take Ukraine into account when planning their work and to consider relevant opportunities for involving Ukrainian actors in Actions and cooperation activities.

title: Programming for 2028-2034 happens now – and the Strategy is here to support!
content:
While we have 1.5 years left of the current EU programme period, the preparatory work for the post-2027 period is in full swing. Authorities are currently mapping the needs to enable the definition of the most relevant thematic focus areas for the funding programmes. The EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region Action Plan provides a solid starting point for the needs assessments.

Over the autumn of 2026, the Strategy Secretariat organises a series of thematic dialogues which bring together funding programmes and the thematic Coordinators of the Strategy. These meetings are the platform for the programme authorities in the region to come together and establish a shared understanding of common needs and challenges across the Baltic Sea Region. The aim is to facilitate cross-fertilisation with national programming processes and the preparation of National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs), including the Interreg Plan and Chapters.

The dialogues also contribute to building synergies among programmes and with Policy Area Coordinators, and lay the groundwork for joint implementation, including coordinated or synchronised calls.

title: Young Planners Work Towards Spatial Planning Challenges in the Baltic Sea Region: Insights from VASAB Young Planners’ Summer School 2026
content:
From 23 to 29 August 30 young professionals and students from across the Baltic Sea Region and Ukraine came together in Gdańsk, Poland, for a week of learning, exchange and collaboration, to explore emerging spatial planning challenges, share ideas and shape solutions for the future of our region.

Participants were allocated in 6 groups and developed ideas addressing four spatial planning challenges:

  • Preparedness and resilience
  • Climate change adaptation and mitigation, including green energy investment
  • Connections between people and places
  • Effective use of space, incl. no net land take and multiuse concepts

    • Here you can find all groups’ final presentations, explaining each group’s work and results.

    Among the six outstanding final presentations, the Summer School jury selected the group that made the strongest overall impression with their presentation, “Containing Resilience: A Modern Counterpart to a Historic Icon.” 

    The winning team – from left Hubert Wulbach, Efia Faschina, Ugnė Bačinskaitė, Wiktoria Jędrusik, Polina Dovzhenko, and their mentor Tīna Šipkēvica, Spatial Planning Expert at the VASAB Secretariat

title: Helsinki EPIC Workshop develops three ideas for transnational cooperation on crisis preparedness
content:
On 23 September 2026, the third EPIC workshop brought together members of the NDPHS Occupational Safety and Health Expert Group (OSH EG) and invited experts in Helsinki to continue developing ideas for a future transnational project on workforce resilience and crisis preparedness. The overall workshop concept was developed jointly by the NDPHS Secretariat and Owe Österbacka, Chair of the OSH Expert Group.

The EPIC – “Effectively Prepared in Crisis” project, funded by the Swedish Institute, aims to enhance collaboration on health-related emergency preparedness and crisis response across the NDPHS Partner Countries and Ukraine, while sharing expertise, lessons learned and good practices to strengthen resilience during crises.

title: Good practice from Latvia featured in Interreg Europe’s podcast
content:
Thanks to inspiration from an Interreg Europe project, officials in Saulkrasti, Latvia, organised a summer camp for Ukrainian refugee to children to connect with locals. The experience was recently focused on Interreg Europe’s podcast.

When Russia’s war against Ukraine began in 2022, the Saulkrasti Municipality welcomed Ukrainian families, including children who had arrived without their parents. 

Local authorities and schools had to respond quickly, often without previous experience of supporting children displaced by war. They knew they needed to create safe, meaningful and inclusive activities, but where to start? 

The answer came through interregional cooperation. 

As part of the Interreg Europe project SIRM, representatives from Saulkrasti took part in a study visit to Rzeszów, Poland, in July 2023. They discovered initiatives combining language learning, creative activities, sport, cultural exchange and emotional support for refugee children and families. 

Listen to the podcast ‘When Europe cooperates’ and discover how European cooperation helped turn an urgent local challenge into a summer camp bringing Ukrainian and Latvian children together. 

Listen now to the podcast episode.

title: Arts and mental health in wartime: Exchanging experiences with Ukraine
content:
How can arts and cultural activities support people living with trauma, grief, displacement and the continuing pressure of war? And what can mental health professionals across the Baltic Sea Region learn from the experience of Ukrainian communities?

These questions were at the heart of the third international meeting of the Arts for Health and Well-being Network (ArtWell NET), held in Kolomyia, Ukraine. Partners from Ukraine, Sweden, Poland and Estonia came together with local psychologists, educators and cultural professionals to exchange experience and explore how arts-based approaches can support mental health, recovery and community resilience.

For communities in Ukraine, mental health support is needed in circumstances of continuing uncertainty and loss. Veterans, military families, internally displaced people, children and professionals supporting others may all face the psychological consequences of war.

Clinical services remain essential, but they cannot meet every need alone. Safe group activities, trusted local networks and opportunities for creativity and connection can also help people regain a sense of belonging, express difficult emotions and rebuild everyday routines.

title: Growing interdependence reshapes energy security across the Baltic Sea
content:
This article is originally posted on the Nordic Energy Research website on 22 September 2026.

The Nordic and Baltic countries have spent decades connecting their energy systems. Now they face another challenge: how to protect them together. At the Nordic-Baltic Energy Conference 2026 in Riga, policymakers and experts pointed to concrete areas for deeper cooperation – from joint threat assessments and reserves of critical equipment to cable repair capacity and better information sharing during incidents.

“Geography matters less, interdependency matters more.”

With these words, Karen Ellemann, Secretary General of the Nordic Council of Ministers, opened the Nordic-Baltic Energy Conference 2026 and set out a central challenge for the region: as energy systems become more interconnected, security risks increasingly cross national borders too.

At the same time, rising energy demand and electrification mean that energy systems need to expand while becoming more resilient to geopolitical uncertainty, threats to critical infrastructure and the consequences of climate change.
